Field surveys of a population of Glyptothorax macromaculatus in a hill-stream system of the Western Ghats provided the first detailed life-history data for this benthic catfish. The maximum body size attained by individuals in this population was recorded at 16.1 cm [Li = 16.1 cm], a value consistent with the modest asymptotic lengths typical of glyptothoracine sisorids inhabiting fast-flowing, torrential habitats. Female total length at the onset of puberty was determined to be 8 cm [Lp = 8 cm], based on macroscopic examination of ovarian development in a sample of over sixty individuals. The corresponding wet weight at puberty for these females averaged 4.16 grams [Wwp = 4.16 grams], reflecting the relatively slender body form and low condition factor characteristic of rheophilic fishes adapted to high-velocity currents. The gonadosomatic index (GSI), calculated for reproductively active females collected during the pre-monsoon spawning season, exhibited a mean value of 4.5% [GSI = 4.5%] when assessed at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

A separate laboratory-based rearing experiment, conducted at a controlled temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], was designed to quantify early life-history traits under stable thermal conditions. The period from fertilisation to the moment of eclosion, marking the transition to free-swimming larval life, was carefully monitored. Hatchlings emerged from the incubating eggs after approximately 10 days [ab = approximately 10 days], with chorion rupture occurring synchronously at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]among siblings. The mean wet weight at birth for these newly emerged yolk-sac larvae was determined to be 0.0018 grams [Wwb = 0.0018 grams], a minute mass derived from the initial egg diameter of roughly 1.5 mm. This value places the species among those producing small, moderately yolk-laden eggs typical of broadcast spawners with a relatively short endotrophic phase. The larvae remained in a non-feeding, lecithotrophic state for the first several days following hatching, absorbing their yolk reserves before the onset of first exogenous feeding. The point of no return, after which starved larvae could no longer initiate feeding, was also recorded during this observational period.

The maximum longevity of Glyptothorax macromaculatus was investigated through mark-recapture studies and the analysis of opercular bone microstructures. The oldest documented individual from the field population was estimated to have survived for 3,650 days [am = 3,650 days] under natural stream conditions at a mean annual water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This substantial lifespan, exceeding ten years, is noteworthy for a fish of its modest ultimate body size and suggests a relatively slow pace of life, possibly linked to the energetic constraints of occupying a high-oxygen-demand environment. Such longevity places the species among the longer-lived members of the Sisoridae, a family generally characterised by delayed maturation and extended reproductive windows in their native torrent habitats. Repeated captures of known individuals over consecutive monsoon seasons indicated strong site fidelity. The growth increments observed in recaptured specimens suggested a decelerating growth trajectory that approached the asymptotic length relatively late in life, a pattern consistent with the comparatively old age at which individuals achieve their final body dimensions.

Comparative morphometric analysis of the ovarian development series provided further insight into the relationship between body size and reproductive status. Data indicated that females attaining a wet weight of 4.16 grams [Wwp = 4.16 grams] consistently exhibited the first signs of vitellogenesis, confirming the tight coupling between somatic mass and the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis. In contrast, the theoretical maximum adult wet weight, estimated from the length-weight relationship derived for this population, was calculated to be 33.9 grams [Wwi = 33.9 grams]. This value, representing the asymptotic wet weight, is consistent with the 0.00813*L^3.00 scaling observed across the size range of collected adults. The substantial difference between the weight at puberty and the ultimate weight indicates a prolonged period of post-maturational somatic growth, during which females continue to increase in body mass by a factor of roughly eight before reaching their final adult dimensions. This pattern is adaptive in environments where fecundity is positively correlated with maternal body size, allowing for greater lifetime reproductive output as individuals age.

The interplay between individual growth rates and the thermal regime of the natal stream was further explored through an examination of age-length relationships. The maximum body length of 16.1 cm [Li = 16.1 cm] was rarely attained by fish younger than eight years, suggesting that the asymptotic size is approached slowly in this environment. When considering the entire life history from the moment of hatching, the median time required for a newly emerged larva to achieve the pubertal length of 8 cm [Lp = 8 cm] was estimated at roughly three to four years under the prevailing thermal conditions. This slow maturation, combined with the extended reproductive lifespan, positions Glyptothorax macromaculatus as a K-selected strategist relative to many lowland cyprinids. The species appears to invest in iteroparous spawning events across multiple seasons, gradually building up reproductive biomass. The gonadosomatic index was 4.5% [GSI = 4.5%] at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].
